title: Job 6:11–20
context: Job continues speaking. He has no strength left to wait and no hope of an end that would make patience worthwhile; he is not made of stone or bronze (6:11–13). He then turns to his friends: kindness should be shown to the one who is ready to faint, even if he forsakes the fear of the Almighty (6:14). The sense of the second half of 6:14 is debated, and this page does not settle it. Job compares his friends to seasonal streams that swell with melting ice and snow but vanish in the heat, leaving caravans from Tema and Sheba disappointed and lost in the waste (6:15–20). Both traditions read the unit as a lament about the failure of friends in a time of need, and as a reminder that the despairing are owed kindness, while not turning Job’s complaint into a lesson against him.

verses.text: What is my strength, that I should wait? What is my end, that I should be patient?
verses.arminianNotes: “What is my strength, that I should wait?” Arminian readers hear a man whose endurance is exhausted. Job is not refusing patience out of rebellion; he simply has no strength left and sees no end that would make waiting bearable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear honest exhaustion. They note that Eliphaz had urged patient acceptance, and Job replies that he lacks the strength for it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with compassion and recognize that suffering can drain a person’s capacity to hope.

verses.text: Is my strength the strength of stones? Or is my flesh of bronze?
verses.arminianNotes: “Is my strength the strength of stones? Or is my flesh of bronze?” Arminian readers note Job’s reminder that he is human and frail. Those who counsel sufferers must remember that they are speaking to flesh and blood, not to stone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a plea for his friends to recognize his frailty. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a call to compassion and as a reminder that human beings have real limits under suffering, which faithful friends should respect.

verses.text: Isn’t it that I have no help in me, that wisdom is driven away from me?
verses.arminianNotes: Job has no help in himself, and wisdom has been driven from him. Arminian readers hear the depth of his helplessness. He cannot find resources within himself to cope, and he says so plainly, without pretending to strength he does not have.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a man brought to the end of his own resources. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as honest lament and see in it the kind of helplessness that calls for patient, compassionate support rather than quick answers.

verses.text: “To him who is ready to faint, kindness should be shown from his friend; even to him who forsakes the fear of the Almighty.
verses.arminianNotes: “To him who is ready to faint, kindness should be shown from his friend.” Arminian readers note Job’s appeal to the loyal kindness friends owe one another, especially to the despairing. The second half of the verse is debated, and they hold its sense loosely.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a just claim on friendship and recall the proverb “A friend loves at all times” (Proverbs 17:17). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as affirming that kindness is owed to the despairing, and neither turns the uncertain second clause into a judgment on Job.

verses.text: My brothers have dealt deceitfully as a brook, as the channel of brooks that pass away;
verses.arminianNotes: Job says his brothers have dealt deceitfully like a brook, like seasonal channels that pass away. Arminian readers note the sharp image of friends who promise refreshment and then disappear. Job feels betrayed by those he expected to help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the pain of disappointed friendship. Shared ground: both traditions read the image as Job’s honest complaint about his friends, reporting it as his perception without deciding the whole case against them at this point in the book.

verses.text: which are black by reason of the ice, in which the snow hides itself.
verses.arminianNotes: The streams are dark with ice, where snow hides itself. Arminian readers note the vivid picture of a stream swollen in the cold season. It looks abundant and reliable, which makes its later failure all the more disappointing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as part of the extended image of seasonal streams. Shared ground: both traditions read it as poetry describing apparent abundance, preparing for the contrast with the dry season in the next verse.

verses.text: In the dry season, they vanish. When it is hot, they are consumed out of their place.
verses.arminianNotes: In the dry season the streams vanish; in the heat they are consumed. Arminian readers note that the streams fail exactly when they are most needed. Job feels that his friends have failed him in the same way, in the time of his greatest need.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the point of the image: help that disappears in the heat is no help at all. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as poetic lament about failed support, and both see in it a warning for those who would comfort the suffering.

verses.text: The caravans that travel beside them turn away. They go up into the waste, and perish.
verses.arminianNotes: Caravans that travel beside the streams turn aside, go up into the waste, and perish. Arminian readers note the tragic consequence of trusting a source that fails. The image shows how deeply Job feels let down by those he relied on.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as heightening the image of disappointed hope. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as poetry, without pressing geographic details, and see in it the seriousness of failing those who depend on us.

verses.text: The caravans of Tema looked. The companies of Sheba waited for them.
verses.arminianNotes: The caravans of Tema and the companies of Sheba looked and waited for the water. Arminian readers note the expectancy of travelers depending on the streams. Job, too, had hoped for refreshment from his friends.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the names as caravans of trading peoples, without pressing the identifications. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Job’s poetic picture of hope that is disappointed, and see no doctrinal question in the place names.

verses.text: They were distressed because they were confident. They came there, and were confounded.
verses.arminianNotes: The travelers were distressed because they had been confident; they came and were confounded. Arminian readers note the bitterness of hope betrayed. The deeper the trust, the sharper the disappointment, and Job feels this keenly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the pain of misplaced confidence and see the image completed. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the climax of the stream image and as Job’s honest description of how his friends’ failure has affected him.
